neighbours.label: a citation of the book of Isaiah: the token after 'Isaiah'/'Isa.' before the chapter number
fire: God promises new heavens and a new earth (Isaiah 65:17), not a slow process.
The prophet speaks of the return of the exiles in Isaiah 11:11.
By his wounds we are healed (Isa. 53:5), the preacher reminded them.
Look at Isaiah 62:4, where the land is given a new name.
The earth will give birth to her dead, as Isaiah 26:19 says.
Many sermons on hope begin with Isaiah 40:31 and the image of eagles.
The Messianic era is described in Isaiah 2:4, where swords become ploughshares.
Compare the servant songs in Isaiah 42:1 with the gospel accounts.
quiet: God promises a future and a hope (Jeremiah 29:11), not a slow decline.
The prophet speaks of the return of the exiles in Ezekiel 37:21.
The Lord is my shepherd (Ps. 23:1), the preacher reminded them.
Look at Genesis 12:2, where Abram is given a great promise.
The dry bones will live again, as Ezekiel 37:5 says.
Many sermons on hope begin with Romans 8:28 and the promise of good.
The Messianic era is described in Micah 4:3, where swords become ploughshares.
Compare the psalms of lament in Psalm 22:1 with the gospel accounts.

notes: 13 of top 32 peak on the space after 'Isaiah'.
